question: Which bacterium causes General Paralysis of the Insane (GPI)?
explanation: You got this! GPI is a serious neurological condition that happens when a syphilis infection caused by Treponema pallidum is left untreated for a long time. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T1#GNS222_U4_T1_h1)

question: How does General Paralysis of the Insane (GPI) usually show up in a patient?

options.A: It strikes suddenly right after a head injury.
options.B: It appears a few days after a bad cough or cold.
options.C: It is passed down directly from parents to children in their genes.
options.D: It develops many years after an untreated syphilis infection.

explanation: Spot on! GPI is a late complication of neurosyphilis that quietly creeps in years or even decades after the initial infection was missed or left untreated. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T1#GNS222_U4_T1_h1)

question: Which parts of the brain are hit hardest by GPI?
explanation: Great job! The frontal and temporal lobes bear the brunt of the inflammation in GPI, which explains why patients experience major shifts in personality and memory loss. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T1#GNS222_U4_T1_h2)

question: What major physical change happens inside the brain during late-stage GPI?

options.A: Nerve fibers rapidly grow too thick and strong.
options.B: Brain tissue shrinks and nerve cells are lost.
options.C: Pus and fluid swell up inside the ventricles.
options.D: Fatty plaques build up in large clumps.

explanation: You nailed it! Long-term inflammation slowly destroys brain cells, leading to a noticeable shrinking of the brain known as cerebral atrophy. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T1#GNS222_U4_T1_h2)

question: What kind of thinking or belief is a classic sign of a patient with GPI?

options.A: Hearing strangers whispering secrets all day
options.B: Washing their hands constantly out of fear of germs
options.D: Grandiose delusions, like believing they own the whole world

explanation: That's right! Patients with GPI often have huge, unrealistic beliefs about themselves, such as thinking they are multi-millionaires, royalty, or even gods. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T1#GNS222_U4_T1_h3)

question: When talking to a patient with GPI, what speech and facial sign might you notice?

options.A: They cannot make any sound at all.
options.B: They stutter rapidly only when they are stressed.
options.C: Slurred speech with trembling around the lips.
options.D: They suddenly switch to speaking a foreign language.

explanation: Spot on! Nerve damage affects the tiny muscles of the mouth and tongue, causing mild tremors and classic slurred speech. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T1#GNS222_U4_T1_h3)

question: Which test is most important to confirm that syphilis has reached the brain?

options.A: Lumbar puncture to check the cerebrospinal fluid
options.C: An EEG to check brain waves

explanation: Brilliant! A lumbar puncture lets doctors test the fluid around the brain and spinal cord for signs of infection and antibodies. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T1#GNS222_U4_T1_h4)

question: Why do doctors order an MRI or CT scan for a patient suspected of having GPI?

options.A: To check the exact amount of bacteria floating in the blood
options.B: To see how well the patient's body handles penicillin
options.C: To check for brain shrinkage and rule out other causes of dementia
options.D: To prove the patient has a brand-new skin sore from syphilis

explanation: You got it! Brain scans help us spot shrinkage (atrophy) and make sure the symptoms aren't coming from a stroke, tumor, or other memory issues. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T1#GNS222_U4_T1_h4)

question: What is the main medication used to treat General Paralysis of the Insane?
explanation: Well done! High-dose intravenous penicillin G is our top weapon to clear the Treponema pallidum bacteria out of the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T1#GNS222_U4_T1_h5)

question: A GPI patient gets their first penicillin dose and suddenly develops a fever, chills, and worse symptoms. What is the most likely reason?

options.A: Their brain shrinkage is suddenly getting worse forever.
options.B: They are having a bad allergic reaction to the penicillin.
options.C: They caught a brand-new pneumonia infection in the ward.
options.D: A normal Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction as the bacteria die off.

explanation: Spot on! When masses of bacteria die off all at once from the antibiotic, they release toxins that cause a temporary fever flare-up. It's tough, but it means the drug is working! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T1#GNS222_U4_T1_h5)

question: Why is keeping the hospital environment safe such a big priority when caring for a GPI patient?

options.A: Patients go completely blind and cannot find their way around.
options.B: Confusion and poor body balance put them at high risk for falls.
options.C: Patients can easily spread the infection to staff through casual touch.
options.D: Bright lights can trigger sudden seizures.

explanation: That's correct! Because brain changes mess with both thinking and physical balance, our main nursing goal is keeping the patient safe from nasty falls. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T1#GNS222_U4_T1_h6)

question: What is the biggest factor in whether a GPI patient will fully get their memory and thinking back after treatment?

options.A: How many family members live in their house
options.B: Catching and treating the disease early before permanent brain damage happens
options.C: The specific hospital ward they were admitted to
options.D: The patient's age when they were born

explanation: You nailed it! Antibiotics can kill the bacteria, but they cannot bring dead brain cells back to life. That's why early detection is everything! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T1#GNS222_U4_T1_h6)
